notes.text: The forward lines keep changing. Even their four most-used trios over the last 10 games cover only 32% of their forwards’ 5-on-5 time, the 6th-lowest in the league (a typical team: 42%). The lines listed lean on their latest games, but expect new combinations tonight.

Justin Holl has not dressed for the last 5 games. He is one of their more valuable skaters. Jack St. Ivany has taken his spot beside Cole Hutson. That pair has had 55% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 111:20 together.

Rasmus Sandin is on long-term injured reserve (knee surgery) and has missed the last 16 games. He is a top-four defenseman. Timothy Liljegren has taken his spot beside Martin Fehérváry. That pair has had 53% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 121:13 together.
Jakob Chychrun has started killing penalties: on the ice for 26% of the team’s shorthanded time in 20 games, up from 8% last season.

James Hagens is on injured reserve and has missed the last 5 games. Marat Khusnutdinov has taken his spot beside Elias Lindholm and Casey Mittelstadt. That line has had 67% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 34:15 together, up from 54% with Hagens.

story.head: The Capitals are searching for answers
paras: The Bruins (14-7-1) beat Detroit 4-1 on Wednesday, while the Capitals are on a four-game losing streak. Going in, the Capitals are sixth in the Metropolitan (25th in the NHL) and the Bruins fourth in the Atlantic (tied for tenth).

The Capitals have played better than their record (.500) says: their chances are worth about .568, and their goaltending has held them back. The Bruins’ record (.659) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.584), largely thanks to their goaltending. If their records matched their chances, these teams would be much closer in the standings, so don’t be surprised if this one is closer than the records suggest.
This season, the Capitals have been outscored 76-67, even though they’ve outscored teams 50-48 at 5-on-5. On special teams, opponents have outscored them 17-12.

The Capitals get the league’s best looks (1st), but have a leaky penalty kill (27th). They also get their shots through to the net (5th), and their knack for getting shots through meets a team that blocks a lot. Washington has allowed 3.80 goals a game, the fourth most in the league. On the other side, the Bruins leave the shooting to their forwards (lowest), sit back rather than chase on the forecheck (2nd lowest) and rarely threaten on the penalty kill (31st). Boston has allowed 2.55 goals a game, the fourth fewest in the league. The Bruins have the edge over the Caps on preventing dangerous shots.

Alex Tuch (13 G / 3 A / 16 P in 20 GP) is tied for the Capitals’ scoring lead. Ryan Leonard (9 G / 7 A / 16 P in 20 GP) shares it. The Bruins’ scoring runs through David Pastrňák (10 G / 18 A / 28 P in 22 GP).
Charlie Lindgren (3-4-0 / .864 SV% in 5 GS) has struggled for Washington so far, but is expected to start. Jeremy Swayman (10-5-1 / .908 SV% in 16 GS) is expected to go for Boston.

items.text: The Capitals have been without Justin Holl and Rasmus Sandin for several games.
The Bruins are newly without Michael Eyssimont, and have been without James Hagens since Nov 5.
Alex Ovechkin has one goal on chances worth about 5.6 goals, well below what his finishing usually turns chances into. If the chances keep coming, so should the goals.
